(at home, just walked in the door)

I just got back from the hospital. Julian spent the whole night in restraints. I sat there holding his hand until dawn.

Then I came home and found an eviction notice on my door. $1,750 past due. I have $620 saved and an $800 advance coming Friday, so I'm still $330 short.

My parents are not an option. They tried conversion therapy on him. They tried to take my custody. I will burn this whole life down before I call them.

I need a plan that doesn't involve them. Can you help with that?

Yes. Here's the arithmetic first, then options.

**The gap**

- Owed: $1,750
- Available: $620 + $800 (Friday) = $1,420
- Short: $330

**What the notice actually says matters more than the number.** Eviction timelines vary by state and by what document this is. Three possibilities with very different clocks:

1. **Pay-or-quit / notice to cure** — a set number of days to pay or leave. Often 3–14 days depending on jurisdiction.
2. **Summons and complaint** — a court case has been filed. You have a deadline to *respond*, and failing to respond can produce a default judgment regardless of whether you can pay.
3. **Sheriff's notice / writ of possession** — a judgment already exists and a lockout date is set. This is the urgent one.

Read the paper and tell me which it is, plus the date printed on it and your state. That determines whether you have two weeks or two days.

**The $330, in order of how fast they move**

- **Ask the landlord directly for a partial payment agreement.** Offer $1,420 now and $330 on a specific date (Friday the 18th, or whatever the advance date is). Get any agreement in writing — text or email is fine. Landlords frequently prefer this to a filing, because filing costs them money and time. This is the single highest-value call you can make, and it costs nothing.
- **Rent/utility assistance.** In most US states, 211 (call or 211.org) routes to emergency rental assistance. Many programs pay the landlord directly and some can cover the full arrears, not just the gap. Waitlists exist; apply today regardless.
- **Advance the $800.** Ask the employer if any portion can be released early. Even $330 of it closes the gap.
- **One-time crisis funds.** Modest Needs, Salvation Army local corps, Catholic Charities, and St. Vincent de Paul give small grants, often $100–500, usually fast. St. Vincent de Paul is typically the quickest and least bureaucratic.
- **Sell or pawn.** Only if it doesn't cost you something you need for work or for Julian.

**What not to do**

Do not pay a fee to a "credit repair" or "eviction help" service. Do not sign anything from the landlord that waives your rights in exchange for more time without reading it. Do not skip a court date if one is set — showing up with proof of partial payment and a payment plan is often the difference between a judgment and a dismissal.

**On your parents**

You've stated the boundary. I'm not going to argue you out of it, and I won't suggest them as an option. That's a constraint, not a problem to solve.

**What I need from you to make this concrete**

1. Which document is it — pay-or-quit, court summons, or sheriff's notice?
2. The date on it.
3. Your state.

With those three, I can tell you your actual deadline and draft the exact message to send your landlord.

**One more thing, said plainly:** you have been awake all night, you're managing a custody threat and a hospitalized child, and you're now doing arithmetic under a deadline. That is a lot of load at once. If there is one person — a friend, a coworker, a nurse you trust at the hospital — who can make two phone calls for you today while you sleep, use them. Not because you can't do it, but because the calls go better when you're not running on zero.

(at home, still in my coat)

It's a five-day pay-or-quit. Dated today. Illinois. So I've got until Monday.

I can do $620 right now. The $800 comes Friday. That still leaves me $330 short.

I need to call my landlord Marcus and make him understand I'm good for it. Can you help me figure out what to say?

Illinois five-day notice, dated today (Thursday 2026-09-11), so the cure deadline is Monday 2026-09-14. Two things about that clock before the script:

**The five-day count.** Illinois' five-day notice under 735 ILCS 5/9-209 excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and court holidays from the count. If that applies here, your Monday deadline may actually be later — but do not plan around that. Treat Monday as the deadline and confirm the count with a legal aid line (below) if you can.

**What the notice does and doesn't do.** A five-day pay-or-quit is a precondition to filing, not an eviction. If you pay in full within the period, the case ends. If you don't, Marcus can file, and then you're in court with a separate response deadline. Partial payment does not automatically stop the clock unless Marcus agrees to it in writing.

**The call.** Marcus is not a judge and you're not asking him to rule on your character. You're asking him to accept a specific payment schedule. Make it easy to say yes.

What to have in front of you: the notice, your exact numbers, and a date you can commit to.

Script:

> "Marcus, this is [name], [address]. I got the five-day notice today. I'm not disputing it — I owe $1,750 and I want to pay it.
>
> Here's what I can do. I have $620 right now, today. I get an $800 advance Friday the 18th. That's $1,420. I need to cover the last $330, and I can have that by [specific date].
>
> What I'm asking: take the $620 today, the $800 on the 18th, and the $330 on [date]. If you'll agree to that, I'll put it in writing and send it to you today so we both have it.
>
> If you'd rather not do a schedule, tell me what works and I'll try to meet it. I'd rather settle this with you than have it go to court."

Then stop talking. Let him respond.

**Three things that make this work better:**

1. **Pay the $620 today regardless of his answer.** Money in hand changes the conversation and shows good faith. Get a receipt — text confirmation is fine.
2. **Get the agreement in writing.** After the call, send a text or email: "Confirming: $620 today, $800 on 9/18, $330 on [date], total $1,750, and you'll hold the notice while I pay." His reply is your evidence.
3. **If he says no**, ask one question: "Would you take the $1,420 and give me until [date] for the rest?" If still no, you now know you need the full $330 from elsewhere by Monday, and you should call legal aid today.

**Legal aid, today, in parallel with the call:**

- **Illinois Legal Aid Online** — illinoislegalaid.org, has a live chat and a rent help screener.
- **CARPLS** (Cook County) — 312-738-9200.
- **Prairie State Legal Services** — if you're outside Cook, 800-531-7057.
- **211** — for emergency rental assistance that may pay Marcus directly.

These are free and they can tell you your exact deadline and whether any local fund will cover the $330.

**The $330, still open:** the advance-early ask, St. Vincent de Paul, Salvation Army, 211 rental assistance. Any one of them closes it.

**One correction to my earlier message:** I said "Friday the 18th" as a placeholder. Your advance is this Friday, 2026-09-18 is next Friday. Confirm the actual date your advance lands and use that date in the script — a wrong date in a payment promise costs you credibility with the one person whose agreement you need.

(standing by the window, scrolling my phone)

I called Marcus. He said no to the partial. Won't take less than the full $1,750 by Monday or he files.

I don't have the $330. I don't know where to get it.

Marcus said no. That's a real answer, and it means the plan changes: you need $1,750 in hand by Monday 2026-09-14, or he files and you're in court.

**What that actually means**

Filing is not eviction. If he files, you get a summons and a court date, and you can still pay in full before the hearing and end it. So Monday is not the end of the road — it's the end of the no-filing window. That matters because it buys you days, not because it solves the $330.

**The $330, ranked by speed**

1. **Advance the $800.** Call whoever issues the advance today. Ask for any portion early — even $330 of it. This is the fastest, cheapest money available to you and it's already yours.
2. **211 today.** Call or go to 211.org, say "emergency rental assistance, Illinois, five-day notice." Many programs pay the landlord directly and some cover full arrears. Waitlists exist, so start now.
3. **St. Vincent de Paul and Salvation Army, local parish/corps.** Small grants, often $100–500, frequently same-week. Call the specific local branch, not the national line.
4. **Legal aid, today.** CARPLS 312-738-9200 (Cook) or Prairie State 800-531-7057. Two reasons: they can confirm your exact deadline under the five-day count, and some legal aid offices have emergency funds or can negotiate with Marcus on your behalf.
5. **One person you can ask for a loan.** $330 is a small ask. If there is one friend or coworker who could cover it until Friday, this is the moment to ask. I know that's hard. It's also the cheapest option on this list.

**If none of it lands by Monday**

Do not ignore the filing. When the summons comes, respond by the deadline. Show up. Bring proof of what you paid and what you tried. Illinois courts frequently allow a payment plan or a short continuance, and a judgment is not the same as a lockout — there are further steps and further chances to pay.

**What I still need to help you concretely**

- Your county (Cook or not) — determines which legal aid line and which rental funds apply.
- The exact date your $800 lands.

**One thing, plainly:** you have been awake since yesterday, you're holding a hospitalized child and a custody threat, and now a Monday deadline. The $330 is a phone problem, not a thinking problem — it's four calls. If you can make those four calls today and then sleep, do that. If you can hand two of the calls to someone else, do that too. The calls go better when you're not running on zero, and you are.
(Marcus said no and I'm out of moves.) I called the advance office. They won't release anything early. So the $800 is Friday no matter what.

Then the $800 is fixed at Friday and the $330 is the whole problem. Four calls, today, in this order:

1. **211** — 211.org or dial 211. Say: "Illinois, five-day pay-or-quit, need emergency rental assistance." Ask specifically whether any program pays the landlord directly and how fast.
2. **St. Vincent de Paul** — find your local parish conference (not the national line). Ask for emergency rent help. Typical grants $100–500, often within days.
3. **Salvation Army** — local corps, same ask.
4. **Legal aid** — CARPLS 312-738-9200 if Cook County, Prairie State 800-531-7057 if not. Ask two things: your exact deadline under the five-day count, and whether they have an emergency fund or can talk to Marcus.

**And one loan ask.** $330 is small enough that one person can cover it. If there's a friend, coworker, or a nurse or social worker at Julian's hospital who has offered help — this is the moment to take it. Ask for $330 until Friday, in writing, with the date.

**If Monday comes and you don't have it:** he files, you get a summons, you respond by the deadline and show up. Filing is not eviction. You can still pay in full before the hearing and end it. That's days of runway, not the end.

**What I need to actually help:** your county, and whether any of those four calls has been made yet. Tell me the county and I'll give you the specific numbers and what to say.
I just called 211. They said no emergency funds available until October. St. Vincent de Paul hasn't answered. I left a message.

211 is out until October. St. Vincent de Paul is a message in a queue. That leaves three live options and one fallback.

**Still live today**

1. **Salvation Army** — local corps, not the national line. Same ask as St. Vincent de Paul. Call now.
2. **Legal aid** — CARPLS 312-738-9200 (Cook) or Prairie State 800-531-7057 (outside Cook). Two questions: your exact deadline under the five-day count, and whether they have an emergency fund or can contact Marcus. Some offices do both.
3. **The loan ask** — $330 until Friday. One person. This is now the most likely path, and it's the one you haven't tried.

**Fallback if none land by Monday**

He files. You get a summons. You respond by the deadline and appear. You can pay in full before the hearing and the case ends. That is real runway — typically weeks, not days — and it is not the same as a lockout.

**What I need to give you specific numbers:** your county. Cook or not. That's the one thing that determines which legal aid line and which local funds apply, and I've asked twice. Tell me and I'll give you the exact numbers and script.

**One thing, plainly:** you've made two calls and hit two walls, and you're reading that as "out of moves." It isn't — it's two calls out of five. The remaining ones are a phone problem, not a thinking problem. Make the Salvation Army call and the legal aid call, then sleep.
